newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: PolyGram exposes music industry woes.
newsitem.headline: PolyGram exposes music industry woes.

text.p: Analysts said on Wednesday that the music industry could be set for a protracted period of stagnation, highlighted by a profit warning from Polygram.

"PolyGram needs to reduce costs further to show a reasonable growth of say six or seven percent in earnings," said analyst Rene Verhoef of NibStrating after the Dutch music and film company said 1996 results would be flat or slightly down on 1995 and that it would take a restructuring charge of $90 million.
In Amsterdam shares in PolyGram, which is 75 percent owned by Philips Electronics NV, were down 5.60 guilders at 79.50 guilders by late afternoon.

Fears Polygram's warning reflects problems in the music business as a whole helped drive down shares in competitor EMI Plc. EMI dipped 36-1/2 p in London to 12.43 stg before recovering to 12.53 stg before the close.

"I do not see the the stagnation as temporary, as PolyGram would have us believe," said Verhoef. High growth rates of the past were over as consumers had finished replacing their long-playing vinyl records with compact discs.
"Margins in the industry are also under pressure as department stores want to purchase music more cheaply," he said, adding that the malaise could continue for several more years.
Jason Crisp, media analyst at Societe Generale in London, said the music business was facing uncertain markets.

"It's clear that a number of markets are growing more slowly than last year," he said. "But what is critical is what is going on at the moment, which is hard to measure. The Christmas quarter typically accounts for about 40 percent of sales and is likely to determine the outcome for the year."

EMI this month denied a report in the Financial Times that fewer platinum, gold and silver record sales awards were given in the third quarter. The company said there was a drop in silver awards but an increase in gold, platinum and multi-platinum awards for higher-selling albums.

Crisp pointed out that EMI could be insulated from any weakness in music sales by its high proportion of music publishing revenues. But he said weakness in the stock also reflected a fading of speculation about a takeover bid following its demerger from the former Thorn EMI in August.

The profit warning at PolyGram for 1996 followed an already marginally stronger year in 1995 when net profit grew to 741 million guilders ($433.3 million) from 738 million as a result of slack pop music sales in the important second half.
In the first half of 1996 PolyGram's net profit grew one percent to 272 million guilders.
"The crucial thing is, will the market pick up?" said Joost van Beek of Van Meer James Capel, who said he was less pessimistic for the slightly longer term.
Van Beek foresaw PolyGram's earnings per share dropping to around 4.00 guilders in 1996 from 4.12 guilders in 1995. "But, in 1997 the figure could rise to 4.50 again," he said.
Van Beek said PolyGram's movie business, still in the red at the moment, could break even at the operating level in 1997.

He said he saw no reason to change his "already low" forecast for tomorrow's third quarter earnings from Philips of a 230 million guilder profit, excluding extraordinary charges -- against the equivalent 1995 figure of 539 million guilders. -- Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000 ($ = 1.710 Dutch Guilders)
